Date: 2026-11-07
Start: 15:00 UTC

Location: Zoom

Attendees: Maya Patel, Jordan Kim (Redwood); Liam Ortega, Priya Rao, Daniel Yu, Asha Menon (Saffron Labs)
summary: Intro discovery for Dedicated capacity: Saffron wants predictable latency for customer-facing chat, 99.9th p99 targets, strong tenant isolation, and a burst strategy to handle marketing-driven spikes. Discussed reserved node sizing, warm pools, KV/prefix caching, network/VPC constraints, encryption at rest, and audit logs. Agreed next steps: Saffron to share traffic profile, Redwood to return cost/throughput options and security artifacts, follow-up demo for warm-pools and KV cache in staging.
topics: Burst/warm pool architecture and prewarm latency
Security: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, SSO/SAML
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Patel: thanks everyone for joining, um we'll kick off in a minute, great to meet you all. this is Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. Jordan my SE is with me.
[00:00:12] Liam Ortega: hey thanks. i'm Liam, CTO at Saffron. we have Priya, Daniel and Asha on too. appreciate the time.
[00:00:22] Jordan Kim: hi all, Jordan here. i'll be focusing on the infra details, sizing, and the warm-pool stuff as we chat.
[00:00:30] Priya Rao: quick context: we run a customer-facing assistant in prod, latency SLOs at p95 < 300ms for short chats, p99 we try to keep under 800ms. volume is spiky - marketing pushes can cause 6x bursts for 10-30 minutes. currently on an in-house GPU pool. cost blew up, ops is near capacity.
[00:00:50] Daniel Yu: and we use a mix of 13b and 70b open models; 70b usually quantized. we do reranking and embeddings also but the assistant is the big cost driver.
[00:01:03] Maya Patel: great, that's helpful. two threads we'll run: first, predictable reserved capacity to cover baseline and part of burst; second, burst / warm pool handling for traffic spikes without full overprovisioning. also isolation - you mentioned multi-tenant architecture?
[00:01:17] Liam Ortega: yes, we host multiple customers on the same cluster but want stronger tenant fencing for regulated customers. basically ability to pin sensitive tenants to private nodes or dedicated vnodes.
[00:01:30] Jordan Kim: ok makes sense. with Redwood Dedicated you can reserve node pools with tenancy controls - we can map tenants to dedicated pools or use hard fencing for specific customers. there are topology options: per-tenant pools, shared hot-pool with affinity, or hybrid.
[00:01:47] Asha Menon: security questions up front: do you support customer-managed keys, HSM or KMS integration? audit logs for inference requests? SSO?
[00:01:56] Maya Patel: yes to all - K M S integrations, HSM options for Private deployments, and audit logs are available via the console and streaming exports. SSO via SAML/Sso is standard for enterprise and RBAC can be mapped to groups. we'll send docs.
[00:02:10] Priya Rao: on performance - how does the warm-pool prewarm work? when a burst hits, we're seeing 5-20s cold-starts with our current infra, which kills conversion.
[00:02:20] Jordan Kim: our warm-pool approach keeps workers prewarmed at the model+quantization footprint, with KV cache primed for recent prefixes if you opt in for prefix caching. typical prewarm to first token latency from warm-pool is < 300ms depending on model size and GPU, cold starts from fully idle can be multiple seconds.
[00:02:39] Daniel Yu: is prefix caching safe for PII data? we have some privacy constraints.
[00:02:45] Maya Patel: good callout - caching can be enabled selectively; you can encrypt cached K V blobs with customer-managed keys and set TTLs. for regulated tenants we can disable caching.
[00:02:56] Liam Ortega: capacity question - what sizing would you recommend for our baseline? our average qps is 18 rps with p50 120ms, p95 540ms; bursts peak at ~110 rps for short windows. models: mixing 13b gpt-style and quantized 70b.
[00:03:15] Jordan Kim: rough thumb - if we assume 13b on 1xA100 equivalent and 70b quantized across two GPUs H100-like throughput, you'd want a baseline pool sized to cover sustained 25-30 rps with headroom. for burst up to 110 rps we'd pair dedicated reserved nodes for baseline plus a warm-pool of prewarmed instances ready to scale. practically that's maybe 8 reserved H100 equiv for baseline and a warm-pool that can add another 6-10 nodes under the burst policy. i'll model exact numbers and return.
[00:03:45] Priya Rao: can we do autoscale on Dedicated or does reserved capacity block scaling?
[00:03:52] Jordan Kim: reserved gives predictable throughput and you can still autoscale within capacity and rely on burst capacity for overflow. Redwood supports autoscale policies tied to queues; if reserved hits limit we can route overflow to a less expensive model variant or to a hosted fallback if you enable it.
[00:04:06] Liam Ortega: fallbacks sound useful - but we need deterministic behavior for SLA customers. if fallback changes model, we need to be sure quality doesn't drop below threshold.
[00:04:15] Maya Patel: agreed - that's why we support canary policy and automatic rollbacks plus evaluation hooks. you can pin some tenants to strict SLOs and never route them to fallback variants.
[00:04:25] Asha Menon: on compliance - we need retention controls for logs and the ability to redact payloads in audit logs. is that supported?
[00:04:32] Maya Patel: yes, log retention and field-level redaction can be configured per-tenant; for Private deployment we can route logs to your SIEM.
[00:04:38] [00:04:38] Daniel Yu: talk about networking - we want VPC peering and private connectivity, no egress to public internet for inference payloads. is Private the only option?
[00:04:47] Jordan Kim: you can do VPC options with Dedicated (customer-managed VPC peering) or Private (full customer control plane). For strict no-egress, Private on-prem or VPC-only Dedicated are the options. we'll map the network constraints in the deck.
  [00:05:00] Priya Rao: what about data residency? some of our EU customers require processing in region.
  [00:05:05] Maya Patel: we have region pinning for models and can pin tenant routing to particular regions. for Private deployments you can also run in your data center.
[00:05:12] Liam Ortega: pricing model - reserved nodes vs usage - what's the delta?
[00:05:18] Jordan Kim: reserved is committed monthly/annual pricing with lower unit cost and predictable throughput. hosted overflow is pay-as-you-go with higher unit cost. We'll send a TCO worksheet.
[00:05:30] Priya Rao: question about KV cache memory - with many tenants, does cache memory balloon and affect other tenants?
[00:05:37] Jordan Kim: we shard KV caches per tenant when using tenant-isolated pools. in shared pools we enforce per-tenant quotas and eviction policies. for strict isolation you can assign dedicated pools which avoids noisy neighbor cache effects.
[00:05:52] Daniel Yu: can we prepopulate KV with common prompts to cut tail latency?
[00:05:56] Jordan Kim: yes - prefix priming and prewarmed cache loads are possible during warm-pool prewarm step; we can script that as part of deployment.
[00:06:05] Liam Ortega: let's talk SLAs - we need 99.9 uptime and p99 latency documented - do you offer SLA credits?
[00:06:12] Maya Patel: yes we have SLA tiers for Dedicated with credits and a support package. for Private we can offer contractual SLAs but need to scope network and infra dependencies.
[00:06:22] Asha Menon: incident response and forensics - do you provide request-level tracing and payload retention window control?
[00:06:29] Jordan Kim: yes tracing hooks, per-request metadata, and you can choose retention windows; for security events we can enable extended retention and export to your logging pipeline.
[00:06:38] Priya Rao: curious about model version pins and rollouts - we can't have surprise model changes.
[00:06:44] Maya Patel: model pins, rollout controls, canary percentages, and automatic fallback are all supported. we'll also surface model perf profiles in the console so you can compare variants before rolling out.
[00:06:56] Liam Ortega: ok, deeper technical - network egress for embeddings, is any 3rd party used?
[00:07:02] Jordan Kim: Redwood runtime is our infra; embeddings can be generated in-cluster. we don't send payloads to 3rd parties unless you opt-in for external connectors.
[00:07:10] Daniel Yu: security again — key rotation - can you rotate K M S keys without invalidating cached K V?
[00:07:16] Maya Patel: we support key rotation with rewrap strategies; cached blobs are re-encrypted on access or via background rewrap jobs depending on your policy.
[00:07:24] Priya Rao: for the warm-pool demo, can we show an example with our 13b model quantized to 4-bit?
[00:07:29] Jordan Kim: yes; we'll spin up a staging instance using a quantized 13b and run a synthetic traffic spike to show prewarm latency and tail behavior.
[00:07:36] Liam Ortega: timeline - we want a pilot before the end of the quarter, ideally two weeks of validation.
[00:07:42] Maya Patel: that aligns - typical pilot is 2-4 weeks. we'll scope a baseline reserved pool, a warm-pool config, and a security checklist for the pilot.
[00:07:49] Asha Menon: what are the minimum enterprise contracts for Dedicated?
[00:07:53] Maya Patel: minimum is usually a 3-month reserved commitment for initial pilots, then commit to 12 months for discounted pricing; we'll put options in the TCO.
[00:07:59] [00:07:59] Daniel Yu: a practical question - where does model quantization happen? on our side or do you handle quantization in the runtime?
[00:08:06] Jordan Kim: we can accept pre-quantized models or run quantization as part of model onboarding. our runtime supports optimized kernels for quantized variants. For critical models we recommend onboarding a quantized artifact to reduce runtime variation.
[00:08:18] Priya Rao: latency SLA again - if warm-pool is primed but cache cold for a new user, what's p99?
[00:08:25] Jordan Kim: depends on model; for 13b-quantized we're usually around p99 ~ 700-900ms with warm-pool but without prefix cache. With prefix priming it can drop under 500ms. we'll show real numbers in the demo.
[00:08:37] Liam Ortega: can you do per-tenant throttles and circuit breakers? we don't want a noisy tenant to degrade the whole service.
[00:08:44] Maya Patel: yes per-tenant quotas, rate limits, and circuit breakers per route. plus we have admission controls to limit per-tenant concurrency.
[00:08:53] Priya Rao: regulatory question: do you support HIPAA BAA?
[00:08:57] Maya Patel: for HIPAA, we have Private deployment options and SOC2 documentation; BAA is possible under Private/Enterprise terms - we'll route to legal for the specifics.
[00:09:07] Daniel Yu: benchmark strategy - can we run a perf test with our payloads?
[00:09:11] Jordan Kim: yes, we'll run a bench harness in staging with your payloads once you share anonymized samples. we'll capture p50/p95/p99 and tail latencies plus token cost.
[00:09:21] Liam Ortega: cost — we need an estimate of token-level unit cost across reserved vs hosted fallback.
[00:09:26] Maya Patel: Jordan will produce a TCO with both modes and show per-token economics.
[00:09:31] Priya Rao: what about burst autoscaling cooldowns? we want a fast ramp-up and gradual scale-down to avoid oscillation.
[00:09:36] Jordan Kim: we support aggressive scale-up thresholds and staggered cooldown for scale-down; warm-pools help remove the cold-start penalty so you don't need extreme overprovisioning.
[00:09:45] [00:09:45] Maya Patel: quick recap before we run out of time: Saffron needs baseline reserved capacity, stronger tenant isolation for regulated customers, a warm-pool based burst strategy with prefix caching opt-outs for PII tenants, and enterprise security (KMS, audit, SSO). Next: Priya shares traffic samples, Jordan sends TCO and sizing, Maya sends security artifacts and contract options.
[00:10:10] Liam Ortega: perfect. any gotchas we should be aware of?
[00:10:13] Jordan Kim: just that actual throughput depends a lot on prompt length and response length distribution; we'll need your token distribution to provide accurate sizing. also model variant changes can shift perf by 10-40%.
[00:10:25] Priya Rao: ok we'll gather that. thanks all.
[00:10:29] Maya Patel: thanks everyone we'll follow up with notes and schedule the demo.
[00:10:33] [00:10:33] End of recording (remaining minutes used for informal Q&A removed from transcript).
